The Anthropic Hiring Process

English · 中文

[!NOTE] Unofficial, last updated September 2026. This guide combines two kinds of information. Statements with a source link come from Anthropic's own pages (careers site, job postings, policies, engineering blog), checked on 2026-09-22. Paragraphs headed Candidates report summarise public write-ups by people who interviewed between roughly April and September 2026; they are not official, they are not linked, and one-off reports are marked as such. Teams run their loops differently and the process keeps changing: your recruiter's instructions and the job posting always take precedence over this page.

At a glance

Stage What happens Length Who gets it
Application Apply online, get referred, or get contacted by a recruiter — everyone
Online assessment One multi-level "build a small system" problem on CodeSignal 90 min many software applicants; often skipped
Recruiter screen Motivation, AI safety, background, logistics 15–30 min everyone
Hiring-manager screen Past work and fit with the team 40–60 min some loops
Technical screen One coding or system-design interview, sometimes two back to back 55 min each most loops
Take-home Performance-engineering and research tracks 2 h to 72 h some tracks
Virtual onsite Four or five interviews (eight in one research loop) over one to three days 55 min each everyone who gets this far
References and decision References, hiring committee, level, team match, offer days to weeks after the onsite

From first contact to a decision: about two weeks in the fastest reported case, one to two months in most, longer when a team pauses or a company-wide break falls in the middle (see Timeline).

Getting an interview

What Anthropic says it looks for

  • "We care about what you can do, not where you learned to do it." About half of the technical staff had no prior ML experience, and about half have PhDs, "but plenty of brilliant colleagues never went to college." (careers)
  • "If you've done interesting independent research, written a thoughtful blog post, or contributed to open source, put that at the top of your resume." (careers)
  • Job postings: "We encourage you to apply even if you do not believe you meet every single qualification." The stated minimum education is a bachelor's degree "or an equivalent combination of education, training, and/or experience". (example posting)

Where and how to apply

Open roles are listed on the careers site, filterable by team and office: about twenty locations in September 2026, among them San Francisco, New York, Seattle, Boston, Washington D.C., London, Dublin, Zurich, Paris, Munich, Tokyo, Seoul, Singapore, Sydney and Bangalore, plus remote-friendly US roles that require travel. Anthropic publishes neither a referral programme nor a limit on how many roles you may apply to.

Candidates report:

  • Applying online works. Several 2026 loops started from a cold application, including a staff-level loop and one that passed the onsite. The first reply came anywhere from the next day (an assessment invitation after an evening application) to two months later.
  • A referral speeds things up but decides nothing. Most referred candidates heard back within a few days, and some skipped the online assessment or even the technical screen; yet one referred candidate failed the recruiter screen and two others their first technical round.
  • Recruiter outreach started several loops, for senior engineers and for a research candidate; one research engineer was referred after meeting people at an AI-safety event.
  • Applying to several roles at once (more than ten in one report) did not prevent a callback. When a role closed before the recruiter got to the candidate, the recruiter pointed them to open roles at another level.
  • The résumé can still be screened after the assessment. Perfect assessment scores were followed by days of silence, and one candidate heard after the recruiter call that the team had passed on the résumé.

Using AI in your application

Anthropic's policy, How to collaborate with Claude during our hiring process (updated July 10, 2025):

  • Application materials: "Please create your first draft yourself, then use Claude to refine it."
  • Take-home assessments: "Complete these without Claude unless we indicate otherwise."
  • Live interviews: "This is all you–no AI assistance unless we indicate otherwise."
  • Preparation: using Claude to research the company, practise answers and prepare questions is allowed.

Some postings still carry a stricter sentence — "please do not use AI assistants during the application process" (example) — so follow the posting you apply to. A few rounds do indicate otherwise: the performance-engineering take-home allows AI tools explicitly, and candidates quote the invitation to the AI-assisted coding interview as giving access to the Claude Code CLI (see Rules during interviews).

Location, visas and hybrid work

  • "Currently, we expect all staff to be in one of our offices at least 25% of the time. However, some roles may require more time in our offices." (posting)
  • "Most staff are in the Bay Area and come to the office regularly. Some live further away and come in for one week a month." (careers FAQ)
  • "Yes. We sponsor visas and green cards for eligible roles." (careers FAQ) Postings add that sponsorship is not possible for every role and candidate, "but if we make you an offer, we will make every reasonable effort to get you a visa, and we retain an immigration lawyer to help with this." (posting)
  • "All interviews are conducted over Google Meet, and we can accommodate a variety of timezones." (careers) No step of the process is in person.

Internships, new graduates and the Fellows Program

  • "We don't currently offer internships." (careers FAQ) Anthropic lists no separate new-graduate programme; recent graduates apply to regular roles, and candidates report new graduates in software and data-infrastructure loops.
  • The Anthropic Fellows Program is the structured entry point for AI-safety research: four months of full-time empirical research with mentorship from Anthropic researchers, a weekly stipend of 3,850 USD / 2,310 GBP / 4,300 CAD and about 15,000 USD a month for compute. No PhD, prior ML experience or publications are needed; fluency in Python, full-time availability and work authorisation in the US, UK or Canada are. The stages are an initial application and reference check, technical assessments and interviews, and a research discussion; cohorts start several times a year. Anthropic says that over 40% of the fellows in its first cohort subsequently joined it full-time, and a posting for the programme's AI Safety & Security track gives 25–50% of fellows in previous cohorts receiving a full-time offer. (announcement, posting)
  • Candidates report the Fellows technical assessments as CodeSignal tests proctored by webcam, with no AI assistant and no web search: one build-a-system test (a DNS resolver in one cohort; completing an inference server inside an unfamiliar, sparsely documented codebase in another) and a separate debugging test.

A public performance challenge

Anthropic has published its original performance-engineering take-home, together with an engineering post (January 21, 2026) on why it keeps redesigning the test as Claude models improve. The repository invites anyone who brings the kernel below 1,487 simulated cycles — Claude Opus 4.5's best result at launch — to email performance-recruiting@anthropic.com "with your code (and ideally a resume)".

Recruiting scams

"Anthropic recruiters only contact you from @anthropic.com email addresses"; in some cases Anthropic may partner with "vetted recruiting agencies who will identify themselves as working on behalf of Anthropic". "Legitimate Anthropic recruiters will never ask for money, fees, or banking information before your first day." (posting)

The stages

Online assessment

Candidates report:

  • Format. CodeSignal, 90 minutes, started whenever you like from an emailed link (one invitation gave a two-week window; another candidate started a month after receiving theirs without trouble). No webcam in the standard version and, in one report, a practice area before the timer starts.
  • Content. One problem in four levels. Each level unlocks when the previous one passes its tests, and later levels extend the same code. The problems are small systems rather than algorithm puzzles: an in-memory database, a bank with two-step transfers and account merges, a task manager, a file system, a recipe manager, cloud file storage with quotas, employee time tracking and pay. Correct, clean, extensible code matters more than asymptotic efficiency.
  • Scores. Partial credit counts: 750/1000 (the last level only partly passing) and 800/1000 both advanced to the recruiter call. A perfect score did not guarantee the next step.
  • Timing and language. The recruiter's email came within a day in several reports, once about two hours after submission. Python is the default; a full-stack role required TypeScript. One invitation offered to reuse a CodeSignal Industry Coding Assessment score from another company's process within the previous six months.
  • Hints. The topic hinted in the recruiter's preparation email did not reliably predict the problem.
  • Skipped in many loops: for some referred candidates, for staff-level roles, in the one performance loop reported and for some research roles.

Recruiter screen

Candidates report:

  • Usually 30 minutes (15–20 in some reports), by phone, with a recruiter rather than an engineer.
  • It is not only logistics. Recurring questions: why Anthropic rather than another lab; why now; what AI safety means to you; how Anthropic differs from other labs; how AI could be misused; an AI problem you think is underrated; what you think of recent company news or the Responsible Scaling Policy. Then your background and the project most relevant to the role, and finally work authorisation, timeline, other processes and sometimes level. A people manager moving to an individual-contributor role was asked about team size and direct reports.
  • It can end the process: in one report a candidate with ten years of experience was rejected after generic answers about AI safety. One recruiter shared reading material beforehand; others outlined the next rounds at the end of the call.
  • Results in one to three days; a promised "within 48 hours" once became an automated rejection the next day.

Hiring-manager screen

Candidates report: some loops put a 40–60 minute conversation with the hiring manager before or after the technical screen — a walk through a past project combined with behavioural questions. Others hold the hiring-manager interview inside the onsite, and a few have none. For one referred senior candidate the hiring-manager call replaced both the assessment and the technical screen, and the onsite was scheduled once it had gone well.

Technical screen

Candidates report:

  • Usually 55 minutes on Google Meet with screen sharing, coding in CodeSignal. Some loops schedule two interviews back to back: coding plus system design, or coding plus a project presentation.
  • Coding problems come from a small recurring set of practical tasks with a concurrency or scale follow-up: an image-processing pipeline, a concurrent web crawler, finding duplicate files, a memoising cache with a bug to fix and durability to add, call stacks from profiler samples, distributed mode and median, a longest-match tokenizer, a boot-program simulator. Until mid-2026 the candidate portal showed a question number (Coding Q1–Q6, System design Q1–Q5); since about June–July 2026 it shows only a general note such as "be prepared to handle concurrency using primitives/libraries of your choice", which does not reliably predict the problem.
  • System design is the first technical round for many senior and staff candidates. It happens in a shared Google Doc or on any whiteboard tool you share. A growing share are design-document reviews: you get a written design with planted problems (for example an inference service that batches requests), a few minutes to read it, and then discuss what is wrong and what is missing. Other recurring prompts: distributing model weights to a large GPU fleet, a prompt playground, a one-to-one chat system, a telemetry pipeline.
  • AI-assisted coding. Since mid-2026 some screens and onsites use a browser environment resembling VS Code and GitHub with the Claude Code CLI available: review several open pull requests in an unfamiliar repository, then improve one. A related format asks you to build an agent loop on top of the Claude API.
  • Research-track screens use a menu of formats; see Research engineering and research science.
  • The editor may start with nothing but a main() function and no tests: you write the file-reading helpers and your own test fixtures.
  • Results the next day in most reports, up to about a week.

Take-home assignments

What Anthropic says:

  • The performance engineering team has used a take-home since early 2024. It started at 4 hours and was cut to 2; it allows AI tools ("For this take-home, we explicitly indicate otherwise"), and its current version uses puzzles on a tiny, heavily constrained instruction set. (engineering post, repository)
  • Other take-homes are done without AI unless the instructions say otherwise. (policy)

Candidates report: research loops use a 4-hour exploratory ML take-home (train and evaluate a basic model, then give a 10-minute presentation) and, in some teams, a 72-hour research take-home; one candidate found that the content differs from team to team.

Virtual onsite

What Anthropic says: interviews run over Google Meet; for technical roles "we use live coding tools like Colab and CodeSignal", and "You can look things up—just be comfortable with basic syntax and standard libraries so it doesn't eat up your time." (careers)

Candidates report:

  • Four or five 55-minute interviews for software roles — coding, system design, project deep dive, culture and hiring manager — on one day or split across two or three; one research loop had eight. One candidate asked for breaks between interviews on the same day and got them.
  • Coding: another problem from the recurring set, with the same concurrency, I/O-versus-CPU and crash-recovery follow-ups.
  • System design: one round in most loops; staff-level loops had two or three, sometimes with no coding at all. The design-document review format is frequent.
  • Project deep dive: present a past project for about 20 minutes (slides or a shared screen), then answer questions on decisions, trade-offs, your own role and results.
  • Culture: AI safety and values — whether you would delay a risky breakthrough and what if others do not or you fall behind, what you would do if the company's stock fell to zero, what you disagree with in Anthropic's approach to safety, stories about changing your mind or repairing a working relationship. The interviewer is not necessarily an engineer. Several candidates whose technical rounds felt fine believed the culture round decided against them; in one case where the recruiter did explain the rejection, the deciding round was a technical one.
  • Hiring manager (if not held earlier): impact, collaboration, growth, team fit.
  • Track-specific rounds: performance modelling (roofline estimates for matrix multiplications and sharding in a spreadsheet-like tool), a network-debugging role play and distributed coding for performance and infrastructure roles; AI-assisted pull-request review; research coding and debugging, such as a GRPO training loop.
  • A recruiter added an extra culture interview when the first one's signal was not strong enough (single report), and one recruiter warned that a poor first day could cancel the second.
  • One candidate reported that each interview gets a numeric rating, that a single 2 usually ends the loop and that passing takes mostly 3s and 4s (unverified).

References, levelling, team match and offer

What Anthropic says:

  • Anthropic's applicant privacy notice for Australia, Japan, Singapore, South Korea, Switzerland, the UK and the EU (October 2025) states that it "may contact your professional and academic referees to confirm the employment, professional and academic information that you have provided", that "if we decide to offer you employment" it may also collect verification of your employment history and professional qualifications from third parties, and that criminal background checks are reported "pass / fail only". (notice)
  • Postings: "Years of experience required will correlate with the internal job level requirements for the position." (posting)
  • On offers: "Take your time. We're happy to give you space to think and finish any other interview processes you're going through." (careers FAQ)

Candidates report:

  • References are requested after the onsite, from the next day to a week later — two in the reports that give a number, in one case a former manager and a current colleague. Rejections still followed some reference checks.
  • One recruiter said the level is set at the hiring committee after the loop, not before it.
  • Some loops interview for one team; in others (general hiring) team matching comes after the onsite. Candidates passed every interview and then failed team matching. Two candidates had all-positive feedback and no offer because the team wanted someone more experienced; for one of them, who had interviewed for a single team, no cooldown applied. In another loop the team chose a different candidate and the recruiter looked for other teams.
  • Equity is a large part of the package, and its price was said to follow the offer-signing date relative to the latest funding round (unverified).

Timeline

Candidates report:

Step Reported range
Application → first contact next day to about two months
Assessment submitted → recruiter email about two hours to a few days
Result of a round next day to about a week
Gap between rounds a few days to three weeks
Onsite → decision one to five days; longer when team matching is involved
End to end about two weeks (fastest) to two months
  • Fastest reported loop (research, recruiter outreach): recruiter contact on day 1, hiring manager on day 4, a two-day onsite on days 10–11, references requested on day 13, the decision on day 15.
  • A staff-level loop from a referral: application on day 1, recruiter call on day 6, system-design screen on day 20 after a week-long company break, a two-day onsite on days 35–36, decision on day 38.
  • Company-wide breaks pause recruiting: a week-long summer break held up several loops, and one report put slow replies down to an internal hack week.
  • With a competing offer, one candidate asked on a Monday to speed things up and had the onsite that Thursday and Friday.
  • One candidate read a rejection that came about a week after a round as meaning that no team had picked them up, not that the round had failed (their own interpretation).

Tracks

Software engineering (product and infrastructure)

Candidates report this typical order: online assessment → recruiter screen → technical screen (coding, system design or both) → onsite (coding, system design, project deep dive, culture, hiring manager) → references → team match → offer. Product loops drew the prompt-playground design; infrastructure loops leaned on distributed coding and infrastructure design (weight distribution, inference serving, telemetry). One recruiter switched a system-design slot to a data-infrastructure version because of the candidate's background, and a full-stack role required TypeScript in the assessment.

Staff and above

Candidates report: staff-level loops often skip the assessment and open with a system-design interview; onsites had two or three system-design rounds and sometimes no coding; a recruiter asked a people manager about team size and comfort with an individual-contributor role; one team was hiring only at "Staff+", with a posting asking for eight or more years of experience.

Research engineering and research science

Candidates report applying to a specific team, then one first technical round chosen from a menu (sometimes the recruiter email offers the choice): building an agent with tool use on the Claude API; prompting and engineering with LLMs; coding and design (for example a weighted data batcher); an ML configuration system; ML research fundamentals (coding in PyTorch, with basic linear algebra and plotting); RL fundamentals (debugging a GRPO training loop); or a take-home in place of the live screen. Onsites add research coding and debugging to the culture and hiring-manager rounds; one research loop had eight interviews over two days.

Performance engineering

Postings list Performance Engineer roles in San Francisco, New York and Seattle, with a posted range of $280,000–$850,000 (posting). The team has used its take-home since early 2024 (engineering post); see Take-home assignments. Candidates report (one performance loop): no assessment; recruiter screen, hiring-manager screen, then a coding screen on distributed mode and median; the candidate portal described an onsite with system design framed around performance bounds derived from first principles and a network-debugging role play. An infrastructure onsite had performance modelling (roofline arithmetic for matrix multiplications and sharding), distributed coding and culture.

Anthropic Fellows

See Internships, new graduates and the Fellows Program: application and reference check, proctored CodeSignal assessments, interviews, then a research discussion.

Levels and compensation

Titles and levels

Postings use functional titles — Software Engineer, Research Engineer, Research Scientist, Performance Engineer — sometimes with a seniority qualifier such as Staff or Staff+, and they refer to "internal job level requirements" without publishing the ladder. Candidates report (one discussion) numbered internal levels and a rough mapping in which an Anthropic level corresponds to one level higher at Google or Meta; the mappings given conflict, so treat them as hearsay. Because the level may be decided only after the interviews, ask the recruiter early which levels the role is scoped for. Crowd-sourced compensation by level: levels.fyi.

Posted salary ranges

US postings state an annual salary range (for sales roles, on-target earnings). The ranges are wide, and postings do not say how a range maps to internal levels. Examples, checked on 2026-09-22:

Role Location Annual salary (USD)
Software Engineer, Product (Full Stack) San Francisco, New York 405,000 – 485,000
Software Engineer, Research Infrastructure San Francisco, New York 405,000 – 625,000
Software Engineer, RL Data San Francisco, New York 320,000 – 485,000
Research Engineer, Interpretability San Francisco 315,000 – 560,000
Research Scientist, Frontier Red Team (Emerging Risks) San Francisco 320,000 – 850,000
Performance Engineer San Francisco, New York, Seattle 280,000 – 850,000

A Zurich research posting checked on the same day listed no range. Postings come and go; open the current ones for up-to-date numbers.

Benefits and equity

The careers page lists salary and equity packages; optional equity donation matching at 1:1, up to 25% of the equity grant; 22 weeks of paid parental leave; health, dental and vision insurance including dependents; fertility benefits; flexible paid time off; retirement plans with matching; a $500 monthly wellness stipend; education, home-office, commuter and relocation support; and meals in the office. Anthropic is a private company, so ask how the equity is valued and when it can be sold.

Rules during interviews

Topic What applies
Video Google Meet (careers); candidates report sharing their screen
Coding environment CodeSignal or Colab (careers); for AI-assisted rounds a browser environment resembling VS Code and GitHub (candidates report)
Looking things up Allowed: "You can look things up" (careers); candidates report copying code found by ordinary web search was accepted
AI assistants Not allowed unless indicated (policy); allowed in the performance take-home (engineering post) and, candidates report, in the AI-assisted coding round. Candidates also report being asked to scroll past a search engine's AI summary
Language Python is the safe choice; candidates report Java and TypeScript for several coding problems when agreed with the recruiter beforehand, while some rounds are Python-only
Tests Often none provided: write your own fixtures and run them (candidates report)
Design rounds A shared Google Doc or any whiteboard tool you share (Excalidraw and Figma were used); design-document reviews need no diagram (candidates report)

After a decision

  • "We're not able to provide feedback on resumes or interviews." (careers FAQ) Candidates report template emails, usually one to three days after the last round.
  • "Yes—you're welcome to re-apply after 12 months, or sooner if something materially changes about your experience or skills." (careers FAQ)
  • Candidates report a rejection email stating that interview feedback remains valid for a year and is visible to every team, and, in one case where the only reason was that the team wanted more seniority, that no cooldown applied. After a role stopped hiring, one candidate's process was restarted by a different recruiter.
